sectionTitle: Use of amount of substance in relation to volumes of gases (chemistry only) (HT only)

specStatements.text: Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
The volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20o C and 1 atmosphere pressure) is 24 dm³ .
The volumes of gaseous reactants and products can be calculated from the balanced equation for the reaction.
calculate the volume of a gas at room temperature and pressure from its mass and relative formula mass
calculate volumes of gaseous reactants and products from a balanced equation and a given volume of a gaseous reactant or product
change the subject of a mathematical equation.

scopeNotes.statement: under the same conditions of temperature and pressure
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every comparison of gas volumes in this content is made between gases held at the same temperature and the same pressure, and the stem always says so. No item asks students to predict what happens to a gas volume when the temperature or the pressure is changed, and no item uses a gas equation, a pressure-volume relationship or the Avogadro constant, none of which appear in this section of the specification.

scopeNotes.statement: The volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20o C and 1 atmosphere pressure) is 24 dm³ .
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only molar gas volume used anywhere in this content is 24 dm³ per mole, and it is only ever applied at room temperature and pressure, which is stated in every calculation stem. The specification gives this figure, so it is treated as a value to be recalled and is never derived. No alternative molar volume at other conditions is taught; 22.4 dm³ appears once, only as a distractor, and is identified in its rationale as belonging to conditions this specification does not use.

scopeNotes.statement: The volumes of gaseous reactants and products can be calculated from the balanced equation for the reaction.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Volume ratios are taken only from the balancing numbers of species shown as gases. Where an equation contains a solid or a liquid, state symbols are printed in the stem so the student can tell from the given equation alone which species contribute a gas volume; no outside knowledge of boiling points is required. Every equation used is balanced, and every equation needed is supplied to the student rather than being asked for.

concepts.term: Equal amounts in moles, equal volume
concepts.definition: Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure. One mole of hydrogen and one mole of carbon dioxide fill the same space at the same temperature and pressure, even though their masses are very different.

The rule that equal amounts in moles of gases occupy equal volumes only holds when the gases being compared are at the same temperature and the same pressure. Comparing a gas volume measured at one temperature and pressure with a volume measured at another tells you nothing about the amounts in moles.
The conditions 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure. It is at these conditions, and only these, that the specification gives the volume of one mole of gas as 24 dm³.

The volume occupied by one mole of a gas. At room temperature and pressure it is 24 dm³ for any gas. The identity of the gas does not matter: 24 dm³ per mole applies equally to hydrogen, to chlorine and to any gaseous compound.

concepts.term: Volume of a gas at RTP
concepts.definition: volume in dm³ = amount in moles × 24. This follows directly from one mole of any gas occupying 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure, so 0.5 mol occupies 12 dm³ and 2 mol occupies 48 dm³.

amount in moles = mass in grams ÷ relative formula mass. This is the first step whenever a gas volume has to be found from a mass: convert the mass to an amount in moles using the relative formula mass, then multiply that amount by 24.

concepts.term: Balancing numbers as a volume ratio
concepts.definition: For gases measured at the same temperature and pressure, the ratio of their volumes is the same as the ratio of the balancing numbers in the equation. In N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, one volume of nitrogen reacts with three volumes of hydrogen to give two volumes of ammonia, whatever unit the volumes are measured in.

Only the substances shown as gases in the equation contribute a volume of gas. A solid or a liquid in the same equation occupies a negligible volume by comparison and is left out of any volume ratio, even though it still counts in a mass calculation.
1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. A volume given in cm³ must be divided by 1000 before it is used with the molar gas volume of 24 dm³, and a volume in dm³ is multiplied by 1000 to give cm³.

Rearranging a formula so that the quantity you want is on its own. From volume = amount × 24 you get amount = volume ÷ 24; from mass = amount × relative formula mass you get relative formula mass = mass ÷ amount. Whatever is multiplying on one side divides on the other.

misconceptions.question: Two sealed flasks at the same temperature and pressure each hold 2 g of gas, one hydrogen and one oxygen. Do they hold the same volume of gas?
misconceptions.correct: No. Equal volumes require equal amounts in moles, not equal masses. 2 g of hydrogen is 1 mol; 2 g of oxygen is only 0.0625 mol, so at the same temperature and pressure the hydrogen occupies sixteen times the volume.
misconceptions.misconception: The same mass of any gas takes up the same amount of space, so 2 g of oxygen fills the same volume as 2 g of hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass is the quantity students actually measure on a balance, so it feels like the real amount of stuff. The specification statement is about amounts in moles, but 'amount' is read as an everyday word meaning 'how much', which students equate with mass.
misconceptions.correction: Read the statement literally: equal amounts in moles. Convert each mass to moles with mass ÷ relative formula mass before comparing anything. Only when the mole figures match will the volumes match.

misconceptions.question: Carbon dioxide molecules are much bigger than hydrogen molecules. Does a mole of carbon dioxide therefore take up more space than a mole of hydrogen?
misconceptions.correct: No. At the same temperature and pressure one mole of any gas occupies the same volume, 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure. The size of the individual molecules does not change the volume of the gas.
misconceptions.misconception: Bigger molecules take up more room, so a mole of a gas made of large molecules must fill a bigger container than a mole of a gas made of small ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer a picture that works for solids and liquids, where the particles are touching and particle size does set the volume, to gases, where the particles are far apart and the space between them dominates.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the specification statement as written: equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions. The rule says 'any gas', which rules out molecular size as a factor.

misconceptions.question: One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³. Is that true whatever the temperature and pressure?
misconceptions.correct: No. The figure of 24 dm³ per mole is given for room temperature and pressure, that is 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure. Equal amounts in moles occupy equal volumes only when the gases are under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: 24 dm³ per mole is a fixed property of gases, like a relative formula mass, so it can be used in any question about a gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number is met as a constant to be memorised and is used in every calculation students see, so the conditions attached to it fade into background wording that is never tested directly.
misconceptions.correction: Say the whole statement, not just the number: one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure. Check the stem says RTP before using 24.

misconceptions.question: What temperature and pressure does 'room temperature and pressure' mean in this specification?
misconceptions.correct: 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure. These are the conditions at which the volume of one mole of any gas is 24 dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: Room temperature and pressure means 0 °C and 1 atmosphere, or 25 °C and 1 atmosphere, so the molar volume must be 22.4 dm³.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet 25 °C as the standard temperature quoted for enthalpy and solubility data, and 0 °C with 22.4 dm³ from textbooks and websites that use standard temperature and pressure. Both get filed under the same vague heading of 'normal conditions'.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the pair together: RTP is 20 °C and 1 atmosphere, and the molar volume that goes with it is 24 dm³. If a source quotes 22.4 dm³, it is using different conditions from the ones this specification sets.

misconceptions.question: Does the 24 dm³ figure only apply to simple gases such as hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen?
misconceptions.correct: No. It applies to any gas. One mole of ammonia, one mole of chlorine and one mole of carbon dioxide each occupy 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: Each gas must have its own molar volume, because each gas has its own relative formula mass and density.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other number students use in mole calculations is substance-specific, so a value that is the same for everything looks suspicious and gets treated as a special case for the gases used in the worked examples.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says 'any gas'. Different gases differ in the mass of one mole, not in the volume of one mole; that difference in mass per fixed volume is what makes their densities differ.

misconceptions.question: To find the volume of 8.8 g of carbon dioxide at RTP, can you multiply the mass by 24?
misconceptions.correct: No. First convert the mass to an amount in moles: 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol. Then multiply by 24 to get 4.8 dm³. Multiplying 8.8 by 24 gives 211 dm³, which is far too large.
misconceptions.misconception: The 24 goes with the number you are given, so volume equals mass × 24.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The molar volume is remembered as 'times 24' rather than as 'dm³ per mole', so the ÷ Mr step drops out whenever the question hands over a mass instead of a mole figure.
misconceptions.correction: Write the units on the 24: it is 24 dm³ per mole, so it can only multiply a number of moles. If your figure is in grams, divide by the relative formula mass first.

misconceptions.question: Once you know there are 0.05 mol of methane, do you multiply by the relative formula mass to get the volume at RTP?
misconceptions.correct: No. Multiplying moles by relative formula mass gives the mass in grams, 0.8 g. To get the volume at RTP you multiply moles by 24, giving 1.2 dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: The relative formula mass is what converts a mole figure into a real quantity, so it is used for volumes as well as masses.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass calculations are met first and practised most, so mass ÷ Mr and moles × Mr become the default moves that get applied whenever a mole figure appears, regardless of what the question asks for.
misconceptions.correction: Match the conversion to the quantity: × Mr gives grams, × 24 gives dm³ at RTP. Ask what unit the answer needs before choosing which one to use.

misconceptions.question: In the reaction CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), does the calcium oxide contribute to the volume of gas produced?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only carbon dioxide is a gas, so only the carbon dioxide is given a volume. Decomposing 0.5 mol of calcium carbonate makes 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide, which occupies 12 dm³ at RTP.
misconceptions.misconception: Every mole of every substance in the equation occupies 24 dm³, so all the products count towards the gas volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is remembered as 'one mole occupies 24 dm³' with the word 'gas' dropped, and state symbols are often skimmed over as decoration rather than read as data the calculation depends on.
misconceptions.correction: Read the state symbols before doing anything. Ring the gases in the equation and use only those balancing numbers in the volume ratio; solids and liquids occupy a negligible volume by comparison.

misconceptions.question: A gas occupies 720 cm³ at RTP. What is this in dm³, and why does it matter?
misconceptions.correct: 720 cm³ = 720 ÷ 1000 = 0.72 dm³, which is 0.03 mol. It matters because 24 is a volume in dm³, so a volume in cm³ must be converted first or the amount in moles comes out a thousand times wrong.
misconceptions.misconception: A cubic decimetre is a hundred cubic centimetres, so you divide a cm³ volume by 100, or you can use cm³ with 24 directly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students generalise from the linear conversion 1 dm = 10 cm and forget that a volume conversion cubes the factor, giving 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.
misconceptions.correction: Fix 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ and check the size of the answer: 24 dm³ is 24 000 cm³, roughly the volume of a large box, so a 720 cm³ sample must be a small fraction of a mole.

misconceptions.question: In N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, does 20 cm³ of nitrogen give 20 cm³ of ammonia?
misconceptions.correct: No. The volume ratio follows the balancing numbers: 1 volume of nitrogen gives 2 volumes of ammonia, so 20 cm³ of nitrogen gives 40 cm³ of ammonia at the same temperature and pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: Volume is conserved when a gas reacts, so the volume of gas you put in is the volume of gas you get out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is drilled hard, and students extend it to volume because both feel like measures of 'how much'. The idea is reinforced by liquid reactions where volume changes are not noticed.
misconceptions.correction: Only mass is conserved, not the volume of gas. Count moles of gas on each side using the balancing numbers; if that total changes, the total gas volume changes with it.

misconceptions.question: In 2CO + O2 → 2CO2, the carbon dioxide molecules are heavier than the carbon monoxide molecules. Does the gas volume therefore increase?
misconceptions.correct: No. Three volumes of gas react to give two volumes, so the total gas volume falls. Relative formula mass has no effect on the volume occupied by a given number of moles of gas.
misconceptions.misconception: A gas with a bigger relative formula mass takes up more room, so making a heavier product increases the volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heavier is confused with bigger, and density is remembered as 'heavy things take up more space' rather than as mass per unit volume. Denser gases feel like they should be more spread out.
misconceptions.correction: For gases at the same temperature and pressure, only the number of moles sets the volume. A bigger relative formula mass means more mass in the same 24 dm³, which is a greater density, not a greater volume.

misconceptions.question: Rearranging volume = amount × 24 to make the amount the subject, is the amount equal to 24 ÷ volume?
misconceptions.correct: No. The 24 is multiplying the amount, so it divides on the other side: amount = volume ÷ 24. A volume of 12 dm³ is 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 mol, not 24 ÷ 12 = 2 mol.
misconceptions.misconception: When you change the subject you swap the two other quantities over, so whatever was on the bottom goes on the top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is learnt as a pattern of moving symbols around a triangle rather than as doing the same operation to both sides, so an inverted fraction looks just as plausible as the right one.
misconceptions.correction: Do the inverse operation to both sides, then test the result with easy numbers: 1 mol must give 24 dm³. Put 24 dm³ into your rearranged formula and check it returns 1 mol.

misconceptions.question: Do you have to convert gas volumes into masses, using relative formula masses, before you can use the balanced equation?
misconceptions.correct: No. For gases at the same temperature and pressure the volumes are in the same ratio as the balancing numbers, so you can work straight from the equation. Relative formula masses are not needed when volume is given and volume is wanted.
misconceptions.misconception: The balanced equation only works with masses or moles, so any volume must be turned into a mass with the relative formula mass before the ratio can be applied.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reacting-mass calculations are taught first and always route through moles, so students assume every equation calculation must take the same path and treat the direct volume ratio as a shortcut that cannot be trusted.
misconceptions.correction: Because one mole of every gas occupies the same volume, moles and volumes are in the same proportion for gases. Apply the balancing numbers to the volumes directly, keeping every volume in the same unit.

misconceptions.question: In volume = (mass ÷ Mr) × 24, how do you make Mr the subject?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply both sides by Mr and divide both sides by volume: Mr = (mass × 24) ÷ volume. For 0.96 g occupying 0.72 dm³, Mr = (0.96 × 24) ÷ 0.72 = 32.
misconceptions.misconception: To move a number across the equals sign you change its sign or move it to the other side of the fraction line, so the 24 can be shifted from a multiply to a divide wherever it is convenient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is treated as relocating symbols rather than as performing the same operation on both sides, so 'take it across and flip it' becomes a rule applied without checking which operation it undoes.
misconceptions.correction: Undo one operation at a time on both sides and write each line out. Then substitute a known case to check: 1 mol of a gas with Mr 32 has mass 32 g and volume 24 dm³, and (32 × 24) ÷ 24 = 32.

mcqs.stem: A flask holds 2.0 g of hydrogen gas, H2 (Mr = 2). Which sample of oxygen gas, O2 (Mr = 32), occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: 2.0 g of H2 is 1 mol and 32 g of O2 is 1 mol. Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
Chosen by students who match the masses, treating mass rather than amount in moles as the quantity that fixes a gas volume.
Picked by students who think the larger oxygen molecules need more room each, so fewer of them fill the flask.
Comes from scaling the hydrogen mass by the ratio of the formula masses twice over, giving 2 mol instead of 1 mol.

mcqs.stem: Two identical sealed flasks are at the same temperature and pressure. One contains nitrogen, N2 (Mr = 28), and the other contains methane, CH4 (Mr = 16). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both flasks hold the same amount in moles of gas
options.rationale: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal amounts in moles, which is the specification statement read in reverse.

options.text: Both flasks hold the same mass of gas in grams
options.rationale: Chosen by students who equate 'the same amount' with 'the same mass'; in fact 1 mol of N2 is 28 g while 1 mol of CH4 is 16 g.

options.text: The nitrogen flask holds more moles because N2 is heavier
options.rationale: Selected by students who let relative formula mass decide the volume, so they expect the denser gas to be packed in more tightly.

options.text: The methane flask holds more moles because CH4 is smaller
options.rationale: Picked by students using a solid-state picture in which smaller particles pack more closely, so more of them fit into a fixed space.

mcqs.stem: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: The molar volume quoted for 0 °C and 1 atmosphere, met in other sources and recalled by students who confuse those conditions with RTP.
The right figure with the wrong unit, chosen by students who do not distinguish dm³ from cm³; 24 dm³ is in fact 24 000 cm³.
A decimal-point slip that survives because the student has no sense of how large 24 dm³ actually is.
The specification gives the volume of one mole of any gas at 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure as 24 dm³.

mcqs.stem: Room temperature and pressure, the conditions at which one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³, means:

options.rationale: Chosen by students who have met standard temperature and pressure elsewhere and treat the two sets of conditions as the same thing.
Selected by students who recall 25 °C as the standard temperature used for other data and then guess at the pressure.
These are exactly the conditions the specification attaches to the molar gas volume of 24 dm³.
Picked by students who treat 24 dm³ per mole as a fixed property of gases, so only the pressure seems worth specifying.

mcqs.stem: What volume does 8.8 g of carbon dioxide, CO2 (Mr = 44), occupy at room temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: 8.8 × 24, from multiplying the mass by the molar volume without first dividing by the relative formula mass.
44 ÷ 8.8 = 5 mol, then × 24: the mass and the relative formula mass have been divided the wrong way round.
The amount in moles reported as though it were the answer, with the × 24 step omitted.

mcqs.stem: A balloon contains 1.2 dm³ of methane, CH4 (Mr = 16), at room temperature and pressure. What is the mass of methane in the balloon?

options.rationale: 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20 mol, then × 16: the rearrangement of volume = amount × 24 has been inverted.
1.2 × 16, from multiplying the volume straight by the relative formula mass and never using the molar gas volume.
The amount in moles given as a mass, with the × Mr step left out.

mcqs.stem: Ammonia is made by the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 20 cm³ of nitrogen reacts completely with excess hydrogen. What volume of ammonia forms, measured at the same temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: The balancing numbers give N2 : NH3 as 1 : 2, so 20 cm³ of nitrogen gives 2 × 20 = 40 cm³ of ammonia.
Chosen by students who assume the volume of gas out equals the volume of gas in, so the balancing numbers are never used.
Uses the 3 in front of hydrogen instead of the 2 in front of ammonia, reading the ratio off the wrong species.
Divides by 2 where the ratio requires multiplying by 2, the standard inversion error when applying a ratio.

mcqs.stem: Carbon monoxide burns as follows: 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). What volume of oxygen reacts exactly with 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide, all volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: Assumes gases react volume for volume, so the balancing numbers 2 and 1 are ignored.
The ratio applied upside down: the 2 has been used to multiply the oxygen volume rather than to divide it.
Halving twice, from students who apply the 2 : 1 ratio and then halve again for the single oxygen atom pair.
The balancing numbers give CO : O2 as 2 : 1, so 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide reacts with half that volume of oxygen.

mcqs.stem: In the reaction 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g), 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide reacts completely with 50 cm³ of oxygen at RTP. Which statement about the total volume of gas is correct?

options.text: It stays at 150 cm³ because mass is conserved
options.rationale: Chosen by students who extend conservation of mass to volume, so no change in total gas volume seems possible.

options.text: It rises to 200 cm³ because CO2 has a larger Mr
options.rationale: Picked by students who think heavier molecules occupy more space, so forming a denser gas should expand the volume.

options.text: It falls to 100 cm³: three volumes give two
options.rationale: 3 mol of gas on the left become 2 mol on the right, so 150 cm³ of reactants gives 100 cm³ of carbon dioxide.

options.text: It falls to 50 cm³ because the CO is all used up
options.rationale: Subtracts the reacted carbon monoxide from the total and forgets that a product gas is formed.

mcqs.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). 50 g of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) decomposes completely. What volume of gas is produced at room temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: Counts the solid calcium oxide as occupying 24 dm³ per mole as well, doubling the gas volume.
50 × 24, from multiplying the mass by the molar volume without converting the mass to moles.
50 ÷ 100 = 0.5 mol of CaCO3 gives 0.5 mol of CO2, and 0.5 × 24 = 12 dm³.
The amount in moles of carbon dioxide quoted as a volume, with the × 24 step omitted.

mcqs.stem: Methane burns completely: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l). 40 cm³ of methane is burned in excess oxygen. What is the total volume of gaseous product at RTP, measured at the same temperature and pressure as the methane?

options.rationale: Adds 80 cm³ for the water as though 2H2O(l) were a gas, giving 40 + 80 and ignoring the state symbol.
The only gaseous product is CO2, formed in a 1 : 1 ratio with methane. The water is shown as a liquid, so it contributes no gas volume.
Uses the balancing number 2 from the water or the oxygen instead of the 1 in front of carbon dioxide.
Halves the methane volume, applying the 2 in the equation as a divisor rather than reading the 1 : 1 ratio.

mcqs.stem: Propane burns completely: C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(l). What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 25 cm³ of propane completely, both volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: Uses the 3 in front of carbon dioxide instead of the 5 in front of oxygen, taking the ratio from the wrong species.
Divides by 5 instead of multiplying by 5, the usual inversion when a ratio is applied without checking direction.
Assumes gases react volume for volume, so the balancing numbers play no part in the answer.
The balancing numbers give C3H8 : O2 as 1 : 5, so 25 × 5 = 125 cm³ of oxygen is required.

mcqs.stem: The volume V in dm³ of a mass m grams of a gas at RTP is given by V = (m ÷ Mr) × 24. Which rearrangement makes Mr the subject?

options.rationale: The correct expression with m and V interchanged, from students who swap the two symbols rather than perform the same operation on both sides.
Moves the 24 from multiplying on one side to dividing on the same side, treating rearrangement as relocating symbols.
Multiplying both sides by Mr gives V × Mr = 24m, then dividing both sides by V gives Mr = 24m / V.
Leaves V on top and pushes everything else underneath, a fraction that looks tidy but reverses the relationship.

mcqs.stem: 0.96 g of a gas occupies 720 cm³ at room temperature and pressure. What is the relative formula mass of the gas?

options.rationale: Uses 720 as though it were dm³, giving 30 mol, so the mass is divided by a figure a thousand times too large.
0.96 × 24, from applying the molar volume to the mass instead of converting the volume to an amount in moles.
The amount in moles reported as the relative formula mass, with the final division left undone.

mcqs.stem: Which of these gas samples occupies the greatest volume at room temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: The largest mass in the list, chosen by students who compare masses instead of amounts; it is only 0.25 mol.
1.0 ÷ 2 = 0.5 mol, the largest amount in moles here, so it occupies the largest volume: 12 dm³.
The largest relative formula mass, chosen by students who expect the heaviest molecules to fill the most space; it is 0.05 mol.
0.2 mol, a middling answer picked by students who estimate from the numbers without dividing mass by relative formula mass.
